transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-18
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: 90 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Sandeep Rao (Redwood SE), Carlos Reyes (Denali ML Eng), Anita Patel (Denali Infra Lead), Jorge Alvarez (CTO), Mei Lin (Perf Eng)

[00:00] Lena: all right everyone, thanks for joining. uh quick intros from our side, i'm lena, i'm the account lead, and with me is sandeep, who will drive the benchmark smarts.
[00:08] Sandeep: hey all. i'll riff on the runtime bits, batching, kv cache, and quant stuff. there's a lot to cover so we'll try to hit the protocol first.
[00:15] Jorge: great, thanks. from denali: carlos, anita, mei here. high-level goal — we want a reproducible comparison vs our in-house infra and a path to validate a private deploy in our VPC.
[00:25] Carlos: (overlap) yeah and the big ask is, we care about p95 latency under 500ms for our short-form prompts and cost per 1M tokens.
[00:32] Lena: perfect, put those as success criteria.

Topics covered (quick): prompt sets, load gen, KV cache priming, batching, quantization, VPC constraints, measurement artifacts.

[05:10] Sandeep: okay starting with prompt sets — you want a representative mix, short-form 20–80 tokens for the UI flows, and longer multi-turns for backend summarization. our recommended baseline is 200 samples per workload class, but ideally 1k if you have it. the key is capturing sequence length distribution.
[05:40] Carlos: we can do 200 now, we have a 6k corpus but it's got PII we have to scrub. question — should the prompts include the exact system prompt? our in-house stack uses a truncation policy that differs.
[05:55] Sandeep: yes include the system prompt that will be in prod. truncation semantics matter for kv caching and tokenization overhead. also note tokenization differences across tokenizers can create small but measurable latency deltas — e.g., different bpe splits.

[10:01] Mei: quick note, our real traffic is bursty — 10 qps steady with 200 qps spikes for a few minutes. we care about tail over sustained bursts.
[10:11] Lena: so load generation should model spike windows, warmup, and steady-state; we'll provide a load generator config where you can set ramp, steady, and spike. we typically run 3x repeats and median the runs.

[15:40] Sandeep: moving to KV cache — two pieces: prefix caching (priming common prompts/responses) and backend tokenizer-aligned kv cache. for LLMs the KV cache hit-rate reduces per-token compute massively on continuation requests. but measuring hit-rate consistently is the tricky bit.
[15:58] Carlos: can you clarify priming? is that the same as pre-warming?
[16:05] Sandeep: related but not identical — priming here means pre-inserting commonly-seen conversation prefixes into the cache so that subsequent user continuations hit. pre-warm is more about generating a first pass to populate caches ahead of traffic. also note we have 'prefix cache' which is higher-level and 'kv cache' which is runtime-level for key/value attention states. sometimes the transcript might say K-V cash or K-V cache, transcription may be weird.

[20:20] Anita: our security team is strict — anything touching KV state must be inside the VPC; we can't send cached states to hosted endpoints. how do you handle that with private?
[20:35] Sandeep: for private we run the runtime inside your VPC, keys and cache ephemeral inside the instance. we have an option to disable persistent KV dumps; by default we don't ship KV off-host. if you need audited dumps there's an encrypted path to your KMS.

[25:00] Jorge: what about batch sizes — our current infra batches aggressively to maximize throughput; p95 suffers. we need guidance on the latency/throughput tradeoff.
[25:18] Sandeep: exactly — we recommend configuring dynamic batching thresholds: target latency budget (e.g., 200ms), max batch size (e.g., 32), and an adaptive hold timer. we'll provide a matrix of expected perf deltas for typical models (small, med, large) and quantization levels. generally, quantization reduces memory and slightly boosts throughput but can add small decoding artifacts; effect on latency depends on kernel implementation.

[30:05] Lena: let's call out the apples-to-apples rules we suggest: same model weights (sha), same tokenizer, same sequence length caps, same batch semantics (how padding handled), same KV-cache policy, and identical load profiles (ramp, steady, spike). any deviation gets annotated.
[30:30] Carlos: regarding same model weights — can we pin to an open model variant? our security folks prefer open weights on private infra.
[30:37] Sandeep: yeah we can test both: an open quantized variant and a float32 private variant. we can also run a fallbacks matrix where hosted calls to a smaller model in spikes.

[34:12] Mei: how do you measure token-level cost? we think in cost per million tokens but your runtime has batching gains which make per-token cost not linear.
[34:25] Sandeep: we report cost as effective compute tokens and wall-time cost. our harness will sample per-request token counts and compute aggregate compute-seconds. we'll include a normalization step: compute cost normalized to a fixed qps/seq len distribution. the important part is to include cache-hit adjusted token counts so continuation requests with kv hits are cheaper.

[40:00] Anita: VPC specifics — we need to know port lists, NAT, and whether your private deploy needs cross-account IAM.
[40:10] Lena: we'll share a VPC runbook. short answer: we need egress to Redwood control plane for telemetry (optional with offline), at minimum private peering, and a set of agent ports (SSH/management) only if you allow the optional managed support. we'll include a hardened checklist.

[45:22] Carlos: about quantization — we saw ~2x memory reduction but sometimes weird decoding slowdowns with certain kernels. can you show us how you select kernels and fallback?
[45:35] Sandeep: yes our runtime has a kernel-selection layer that picks the fastest implementation for given seq len and hardware. for quantized models we prefer int8 kernels where supported; we also run microbenchmarks to pick per-layer kernel choices. we'll include a kernel-report in the lab outputs.

[50:00] Sandeep: one gotcha — padding and batch packing matter. if you batch very heterogeneous seq lengths and you pad naively, the runtime does extra compute on padded tokens. we suggest grouping by length (bucketing) and applying packing heuristics. in our experiments packing yielded 15–30% throughput gains for conversational workloads.

[55:15] Mei: for the lab, can you support reproducing our exact burst pattern including 200 qps spikes? and can we run it inside our VPC or do we need to tunnel?
[55:30] Lena: we can do both. for strict security we do an in-VPC private deployment and run the harness from a bastion in your VPC. alternatively we can tunnel traffic via an agreed-upon secure egress; we prefer in-VPC for apples-to-apples.

[60:00] Jorge: what are typical timeline and outputs for the lab?
[60:08] Sandeep: day 0 — exchange artifacts (prompts, sequence distribution, firewall rules). day 1 — deploy runtime in private mode, smoke tests. day 2 — run baseline (no kv priming, default batch), day 3 — run optimized (prefill cache, tuning batching, quantization), day 4 — postmortem and kernel reports. deliverables: raw logs, kernel selection matrix, cost normalization spreadsheet, and an executive writeup.

[65:23] Carlos: remind me on priming — do you recommend synthetic priming traffic to build KV cache before spikes?
[65:33] Sandeep: yes, synthetic priming is standard. but you must ensure it's the same distribution. otherwise you bias cache-hit rates. also if you prime with too many unique prefixes you thrash the cache. we recommend priming with top-50 prefixes over a 10-minute window before the spike.

[70:05] Anita: any pitfalls when comparing quantized vs fp32 in apples-to-apples? we worry about accuracy regressions and different tokenization rounding.

[70:18] Sandeep: call those out as orthogonal metrics — latency/cost vs quality. include a small eval set for quality (ROUGE/BLEU or human spot checks). when possible, use the same seed and decoding settings; note some quant kernels have different float->int rounding that produces micro-differences. document them.

[75:40] Lena: quick recap and next steps — agreed deliverables: redwood share harness & runbook by 11/21, denali share prompts + traffic profile by 11/20, schedule lab week of 11/24, and prepare KV cache priming plan.
[75:55] Jorge: ok agreed. any blockers?
[76:00] Anita: we'll confirm firewall policy and get you a point of contact for networking.
[76:05] Carlos: i'll get the sample prompt set scrubbed and share SLOs.
[76:13] Mei: i'll prepare a small quality eval set.
[76:20] Lena: great thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invites and the GH link.
[76:30] (meeting ends, casual chatter for a few seconds)

Notes on transcript quality: some product names and acronyms transcribed loosely (e.g., K-V cash, V-P-C, quatization typo). we kept original speaker turn flavor to preserve voice.
